nameStory: Sand dollars get their name from their round, flat shape that resembles a large coin - like an old silver dollar you might find buried in beach sand. The scientific name Echinarachnius means 'spiny spider,' referring to their relationship to sea urchins and the delicate, web-like pattern visible on their shells.
description: Sand dollars are flat, disk-shaped marine animals related to sea urchins and sea stars. Living sand dollars are covered in tiny, velvety spines and are typically purple, brown, or greenish in color. They're usually 2-4 inches across and about as thick as a cookie. Most beachcombers find their bleached white skeletons (called tests) washed up on shore rather than the living animals.

idTips.label: Five-petaled flower pattern
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive five-pointed star or flower pattern on the top surface - it feels like raised ridges you can trace with your finger and looks like nature carved a perfect botanical design into the shell

idTips.label: Flat, round disk shape
idTips.description: Perfectly circular and remarkably flat, like someone pressed a sea urchin under a heavy book - about the thickness of a thick cookie or thin pancake

idTips.label: Fuzzy texture when alive
idTips.description: Living sand dollars feel like velvet or soft suede due to thousands of tiny moving spines, while dead ones are smooth and chalky to the touch

idTips.label: Five holes arrangement
idTips.description: Beach-found specimens often have five oval holes arranged in the petal pattern - these feel smooth-edged and are perfectly symmetrical

idTips.label: Color differences
idTips.description: Living ones are dark purple, brown, or greenish, while dead specimens bleach to bright white or pale gray in the sun

idTips.label: Central mouth opening
idTips.description: The bottom side has a small star-shaped opening in the center that feels slightly rough around the edges

habitat: Common sand dollars live on sandy ocean floors from shallow tide pools to deeper waters along New England's coast. You'll most often find their white skeletons washed up on sandy beaches after storms, especially on Cape Cod, the Maine coast, and other exposed shorelines. Living specimens can sometimes be spotted in shallow water during low tide, partially buried in sand.

seasonality.spring: Beach-washed specimens become more common as winter storms subside and the first warm weather brings beachcombers out. Living sand dollars begin moving into shallower waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding both living sand dollars in shallow waters and fresh specimens washed ashore. Living ones are most active and easiest to observe during calm, low tide periods.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases the number of shells washing ashore. This is often the best season for collecting well-preserved white specimens as autumn storms churn up the sea floor.
seasonality.winter: Harsh storms frequently wash specimens ashore, though fewer people are beach-walking to find them. Living sand dollars move to deeper, calmer waters to avoid winter wave action.

funFact: Sand dollars can clone themselves! When a sand dollar gets broken in half, each piece can regenerate into a complete new animal - it's like having a built-in superpower that lets them literally pull themselves back together.
confusionNotes: Sand dollars are sometimes confused with sea biscuits or other flat sea urchins, but sand dollars are much flatter and have that distinctive five-petal flower pattern on top. Remember: if it's thick as a biscuit, it's probably a sea biscuit; if it's flat as a pancake with a flower pattern, it's a sand dollar.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that the white 'sand dollars' found on beaches are actually just the skeleton (called a test) of what was once a living animal. The living sand dollar looked completely different - covered in moving spines and dark-colored, more like a flat sea urchin than the smooth white disks we typically see.
compareHints: The common sand dollar is the only sand dollar species regularly found in New England waters, making identification relatively straightforward. It can be distinguished from other flat echinoderms like sea biscuits by being much flatter and having the characteristic five-petal pattern rather than the more irregular patterns found on other species. Unlike heart urchins, sand dollars are perfectly round rather than heart-shaped.
